text:
Education in Poland begins with compulsory education, which includes primary school (starting at age 6 or 7) lasting eight years (grades 1–8), replacing the previous six-year primary school and three-year middle school (gimnazjum) system introduced in 2017. Upper secondary education follows, offering pathways such as general education (liceum), vocational education through technical schools (technikum) or basic vocational schools (zasadnicza szkoła zawodowa), or profiled general secondary schools (liceum profilowane). Students in general secondary schools can earn the Matura qualification, required for higher education. Vocational programs lead to certificates of competence or a Matura after additional study.
Tertiary education follows the Bologna system, with a three-year bachelor’s degree followed by a two-year master’s degree, though some programs (e.g., medicine, pharmacy) take five to six years. Teacher training requires three years at a teacher training college. The grading system at the university level uses a numeric scale from 2 to 5, with 3.0 as the lowest passing grade. Foreign languages, typically English and German, are taught in primary and secondary schools, with a reform requiring students to learn two foreign languages by the end of lower secondary school.
Historically, Poland had one of the most educated societies in Europe, with the Jagiellonian University (founded 1364) being among the world’s oldest. Major reforms in 1999 and 2017 restructured the education system, including the abolition of gimnazjum and expansion of primary school. The 2017 reform also altered the curriculum, focusing on Polish and Eurocentric history, removing references to non-Aligned Movement, and emphasizing political and military leaders. The education system has faced criticism for promoting nationalism and rote learning, though it has improved in international rankings for reading and science. Violence in schools has been addressed through a "zero tolerance" policy introduced in 2006.
